title: Preserving eggs in water glass
subtitle: Storing a summer glut of fresh eggs in sodium silicate solution for use through winter.
excerpt: Water glass is a sodium silicate solution that seals the pores of a fresh egg and preserves it at room temperature for several months. The method was common in Britain before refrigeration and is still useful when hens lay heavily through spring and summer and drop off through winter. Only very fresh, uncracked, unwashed eggs preserve successfully.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, section on egg preservation. Ministry of Food, Preservation of Eggs (1943), UK wartime advisory pamphlet. Gail Damerow, Storey's Guide to Raising Chickens (2017), chapter on egg storage. University of Wisconsin Extension, Home Egg Preservation (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: A thick syrupy solution of sodium silicate in water, traditionally used to coat and preserve fresh eggs by sealing their porous shells against air and bacteria.
The natural cuticle coating on a freshly laid egg that seals the shell pores against bacteria. Washing an egg removes the bloom and makes it unsuitable for preservation.

content.text: Water glass preservation stores fresh eggs in a sodium silicate solution that seals the shell pores and keeps the contents edible for up to nine months at room temperature. The method uses the eggs' natural
bloom

alongside the silicate coating to lock air and bacteria out. It was widely used in Britain between the wars and is straightforwardly practical for anyone with a laying flock that peaks in spring and drops off in winter.
What you need
Sodium silicate solution (
water glass

) from a pharmacy or pottery supplier. The concentration marketed for egg preservation is typically around 40% solution. Dilute with boiled, cooled water in a 1:9 ratio (one part sodium silicate to nine parts water).
A large clean earthenware crock, glass jar, or food-grade plastic bucket with a lid.
Very fresh eggs, collected within 24 hours of laying. Not washed, not cracked, not dirty.
Eggs to use and to avoid
Use only eggs collected within the last 24 to 48 hours. The bloom must be intact.
Do not wash the eggs. Washing removes the bloom and makes preservation unreliable.
Discard any egg with a hairline crack, even a small one. Bacteria can enter before the silicate seals the shell.
Avoid very large or double-yolk eggs: the thinner shell in proportion to volume makes them less reliable.
The process
Mix the sodium silicate solution in the crock: one part water glass to nine parts boiled, cooled water. Stir gently to combine. The solution should be thin and clear.

Lower the eggs point-down into the solution, blunt end up. Point-down is the traditional position and keeps the air sac, which sits at the blunt end, at the top and slightly larger, which some preservers believe delays deterioration.
Ensure eggs are fully submerged. Add more solution as needed. The top egg must be covered by at least 2 cm.
Cover the crock with a lid or a clean cloth. Store in a cool, dark place: a larder, cellar, or unheated outhouse is ideal.
Add fresh eggs to the crock as they come in through the laying season. Top up the solution as needed to keep all eggs submerged.
Using preserved eggs

Rinse each egg under cold water before cracking. The sodium silicate rinses off cleanly. Preserved eggs scramble and bake well. They do not beat to a firm meringue: the whites have lost some of their setting structure over time. For fried or poached eggs where the white must hold a clean edge, preserved eggs are less reliable than fresh.

Preserved eggs used for baking or scrambling up to nine months after laying are excellent. Check each egg: crack into a cup first and smell it before adding to food. A preserved egg that has failed smells strongly sulphurous and should be discarded. Failures are uncommon in properly prepared batches.

attrs.cue: Eggs floating to the surface after a few weeks
attrs.cause: Air has entered through a crack or poorly sealed bloom
attrs.fix: Remove floating eggs immediately: they have failed. Crack each one into a cup and check before discarding. Floating means the air cell inside has expanded, indicating bacterial activity.

attrs.cause: Normal: fine calcium carbonate particles from the shell surfaces dissolve into the solution over time
attrs.fix: This is not a sign of spoilage. The eggs remain preserved in cloudy solution as reliably as in clear solution.
